comments.text:
Unfortunately this is all mostly wrong. You failed to provide a completely definition, and the part you did (the goal) is just incorrect. 

Here is the definition, just to get it out of the way:

The study of the seven classical liberal arts ordered toward higher philosophy and ultimately theology, with a mastery of the canonical texts used in this classical period. 

The goal is not “the development of the whole student.” That could be argued as a property of classical education, but it’s not the end. 

Latin is also not necessary. Classical education is by definition historical. This real education was primarily divided into the Greek east (in Byzantium) and the Latin west. Unlike the west, the east had consistent access to the source texts which came out of Greece and studied them in the original language. Their grammatical and rhetorical arts were richer and more substantive than those in the west too. A student can very much  acquire a true classical education following the pipeline of the Latin west, but the point is the Greek east pipeline does not study Latin and it is at least as much a classical education.  

The “truth, goodness, and beauty” stuff throughout the video is just silliness. It’s a modern slogan that has nothing to do with classical education except in some contrived way. The cliche needs to go. Same with this whole emphasis on the ‘Great Book.’ It’s ahistorical and has no part in the education.
comments.author: @jakelm4256
